question: An 80-year-old man is admitted with a sudden picture of aphasia and right hemiparesis. As background highlights, hypertension, well controlled diet and cognitive impairment in the last year under study by his neurologist. Emergency cranial CT demonstrates a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause of the hematoma?

options.opa: Arteriovenous malformation masked by the acute hematoma.
options.opc: Vasculitis isolated from the nervous system.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "80-year-old man" -> "sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis" -> "left frontal lobar hematoma" -> "amyloid deposits in cerebral vessels" -> "amyloid cerebral angiopathy" -> 85%
CHAIN: "80-year-old man" -> "history of hypertension" -> "chronic arterial hypertension" -> "left frontal lobar hematoma" -> "possible cause" -> 70%
CHAIN: "80-year-old man" -> "sudden neurological symptoms" -> "left frontal lobar hematoma" -> "arteriovenous malformation" -> "masked by hematoma" -> "possible but less likely" -> 60%
CHAIN: "80-year-old man" -> "sudden neurological symptoms" -> "left frontal lobar hematoma" -> "vasculitis isolated from nervous system" -> "unclear association" -> 50%
CHAIN: "80-year-old man" -> "sudden neurological symptoms" -> "left frontal lobar hematoma" -> "brain tumor" -> "no contrast enhancement" -> "less likely" -> 55%
analysis: The patient is an elderly individual with a history of cognitive impairment and well-controlled hypertension. The sudden onset of aphasia and right hemiparesis, along with the CT finding of a left frontal lobar hematoma, suggests a hemorrhagic stroke. In elderly patients, especially those with cognitive decline, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is a common cause of lobar hemorrhages. CAA is characterized by the deposition of amyloid in the walls of cerebral blood vessels, leading to vessel fragility and increased risk of bleeding. This condition is more prevalent in older adults and is associated with lobar hemorrhages rather than deep brain hemorrhages, which are more typical of chronic hypertension. Therefore, the most likely cause of the hematoma in this patient is amyloid cerebral angiopathy.
